title: How to keep sales aligned on priorities: a Mac guide for product managers in 2026
metaTitle: Keep sales aligned on priorities: a PM guide for Mac in 2026
description: Product managers lose hours when sales chases other priorities. Here is what it costs, why it happens, free fixes, and where Lazur helps on a Mac.
intro: To keep sales aligned on priorities, give each priority one owner and keep one shared list where sales can see it. Then write every decision in a log, with its reason. Published research points to unclear decision rights and too many meetings as common causes of stalled teamwork, so start with ownership, not tools. This guide covers what the friction costs, why it happens, and fixes you can run this week on a Mac.
tldr: Give each priority one named owner, and write the owner next to the priority.
Keep a decision log in Notion or Google Sheets with the request, decision, reason and date.
Hold one short weekly sync with sales, with a fixed agenda and written outcomes.
Lazur can explain a thread, point at a field, draft a reply and dictate notes. It does not operate your apps.

blocks.text: What misalignment costs you each week

Misalignment costs time first. When sales and product disagree about what matters, the same question returns in meeting after meeting. Each round uses hours that could go to shipping or to closing deals. Nobody logs that cost, so it stays hidden until a quarter goes sideways.

Start with the numbers that exist, and read them carefully. Salesforce's State of Sales blog says reps spend 60% of their time on non-selling tasks. That figure covers sales reps, not product managers. It does not measure misalignment. Use it as a reminder of how little selling time is left, not as proof of your problem.

Forrester's 2024 Priorities Survey found that 82% of C-level B2B business and technology professionals say their product, sales and marketing teams are aligned. A separate Forrester Q2 2024 survey found that 65% of sales and marketing professionals believe there is a lack of alignment between the sales and marketing leaders in their organizations. The two surveys differ, and neither measures product and sales alone. Still, the gap between the two numbers is useful. Leaders often think things are fine when the people doing the work do not.

HBR's June 2024 article cites Gartner research that 78% of organizational leaders report collaboration drag. The article describes that as too many meetings, too much peer feedback and unclear decision-making authority. The figure comes through HBR's summary, not Gartner's own report, so treat it as cited rather than checked.
Hidden costs that show up in meetings and on your team

items: Re-asked decisions. The same deal request comes back after a no, because nobody wrote the no down.
Roadmap whiplash. Engineers stop trusting the plan when priorities shift between Monday and Thursday.
Blame after a lost deal. A missing feature gets blamed on product timing, and nobody can show the decision.
Credit fights. Forrester's interviews, which covered sales and marketing, surfaced friction, exclusion and credit-stealing.
Worn-out people. Gallup lists unclear communication from managers and unreasonable time pressure among the causes most closely tied to burnout.

blocks.text: Signs your team is misaligned this week
Look for patterns, not single bad days. One awkward thread means little. The same thread every week means the decision process is broken. Use the table below as a quick check before your next sync.

rows: Sales promises a feature on a call
Who approved it? Add the owner to the log today.
The same request returns every month
The earlier no had no reason
Search the log for the original decision and its reason.
Product hears about a big deal after it closes
No shared view of open deals
Ask sales for a weekly list of open deals with blockers.
Priority changes happen in Slack threads
Move the change into the weekly sync and write the outcome.
Both sides say they are aligned
Ask each side to name the top priority in one sentence.
blocks.caption: Common signs of misalignment and a first check for each.

blocks.text: A worked example: the deal that skipped the queue

Say your team agreed that onboarding, billing and admin roles are this quarter's top priorities. On a Tuesday, a sales lead asks for single sign-on for a large prospect. You reply in Slack that it is not a priority right now. The thread ends with a thumbs up and no decision.

On Thursday, the same prospect comes back through the account executive, with a deadline. An engineer starts a spike. The roadmap shifts. Nobody can say who approved the change, and the next sync starts with an argument about what was decided on Tuesday.

The fix is not a longer meeting. It is a log entry with the request, the decision, the reason and the owner. With that entry, the Thursday conversation starts from a record. You can say, 'We said no on Tuesday because billing is still the top priority. We can revisit it on the date in the log.' If the prospect outranks billing, that call is fine. Make it on purpose and say who made it.
Fixes you can start without buying anything

None of these fixes needs a new tool. Each one needs a decision and a place to write it down. Forrester's blog lists four alignment models and recommends choosing one on purpose rather than by drift. Use the steps below with whichever model your company already follows.

items: This week: name owners for your top priorities in one shared place.
Next: open the decision log and add the last two weeks of requests from Slack.
Then: hold the first weekly sync with a fixed agenda.
After that: post what shipped, and the reason for each no, in the sales channel.

blocks.text: Keep the decision log useful for sales

A decision log only works if people read it. Keep each entry short. A sales rep should understand it at a glance. Put the newest decisions at the top, and link the deal name, not the whole CRM record. For a long log, a [table of contents in Notion](/how-to/add-a-table-of-contents-in-notion) helps people jump to the right section.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. It listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. See the [Lazur page for product managers](/for/product-managers) for more on this workflow.

items: Explain a long thread. Ask what was decided and who owns it. Check the answer against the thread.
Point at a field. Ask where the close date or the blocker field sits in a view you rarely open. Lazur circles it and labels it.
Guide a setup step. Ask Lazur to walk you through a Linear label or a Sheets filter. It waits for each click, and you do the clicking.
Dictate notes. Hold fn and speak your decision note. Clean, formatted text appears at the cursor in any app.
Draft a reply. Ask for a short no that names the priority and a revisit date. Lazur types the draft, and you edit it before sending.
Handle reminders. Set a reminder for the weekly sync by voice.

blocks.text: Lazur does not decide which priority wins. It cannot tell you whether a deal outranks onboarding. It helps you find the record, say the decision clearly and send it to the right place. There is a free trial with no credit card, and you can compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing).

Privacy matters here. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Deal records and customer names can still be confidential. Check your employer's rules on customer data before you hold the shortcut over a CRM screen.
Mac tools for the decision log, the requests and the sync

Slack handles the requests. Linear tracks the work that follows. Notion or Google Sheets holds the decision log. Pick one place for the log, because separate logs drift apart. In Slack, use ⌘K to jump to a channel. Our guide covers how to [create a channel in Slack on Mac](/how-to/create-a-channel-in-slack), including when to make it private.

In Linear, add a label for sales requests so they show up as a group on the board. Our [label guide](/how-to/add-a-label-in-linear) shows the steps for the desktop app. In Google Sheets, pick Data > Create a filter to sort the log by owner or by open decisions. The [filter guide](/how-to/add-a-filter-to-a-range-in-google-sheets) walks through a single range.

blocks.title: Jira on a Mac runs in the browser
blocks.text: Atlassian says support has ended for the Jira Cloud Mac app. Open Jira in a browser tab instead, and keep the decision log in one place, not inside Jira comments.

blocks.title: Salesforce's Slack app is legacy
blocks.text: Slack's help page calls the Slack-built Salesforce app now-unsupported. It recommends the Salesforce-built integrations instead. Check which version your team uses before you build a process on it.

If your sales team lives in Salesforce, Productboard's Salesforce integration can show the total deal revenue tied to each feature's feedback. It also brings in account records. Setup needs a workspace admin in Productboard and admin rights in Salesforce. This is Productboard's integration, not Lazur's, so ask your admins before you plan around it.
When sales should win the priority call

Sales sees the buyer. Product sees the product. Sometimes the buyer's need is the most important priority in the room. A large deal blocked by one missing gap may justify moving that gap up the list. The rule is not that product always wins. The rule is that one owner makes the call, once, and writes down the reason.
Mistakes that make misalignment worse

items: Treating a thumbs up as an approval. A reaction is not a decision, so write the decision down.
Keeping the priority list private to product. Sales cannot follow a list they cannot see.
Fixing it with a bigger meeting. More meetings add to collaboration drag, which HBR links to too many meetings.
Blaming sales for chasing deals. Their targets are their job. Your job is making the trade-off visible.
Buying a tool before you agree on priorities. A tool stores the disagreement just as well as it stores agreement.
Pasting customer records into a screenshot without checking the rules. Check your employer's rules first.

blocks.text: What to do this week

Start with one priority and one owner. Skip the tool search for now. Book the first weekly sync this week, and invite the sales lead who sends the most requests. Bring the priority list. Ask one question: which open deal is most blocked by a product decision? Write the answer in the log before the meeting ends.
When the fix is a people problem

Sometimes the process is fine and a person keeps going around it. Forrester's interviews surfaced credit-stealing and exclusion. A log does not fix that alone. Raise it with the manager on each side, and keep the facts in the log. Stick to dates, decisions and reasons when you talk about it.

faq.question: Is sales misalignment the same as sales and marketing misalignment?
faq.answer: No. Most of the widely cited survey figures cover sales and marketing leaders, or C-level leaders overall. Read them as context for the pattern, not as measures of product and sales friction.

faq.question: What do I do first if sales ignores the priority list?
faq.answer: Ask the sales lead for their most important open deal, then check whether it appears on your list. If it does not, ask what would change that. Write the answer down and bring it to the weekly sync.

faq.question: Who should own priorities, product or sales?
faq.answer: There is no universal answer. Forrester's blog says leaders should choose an alignment model on purpose. Product usually owns the roadmap, and sales should make the case for deals that depend on a gap. Write the split down so both sides can see it.

faq.question: Can Lazur pull deal data out of Salesforce for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur sees what is on your screen while you hold the shortcut. It can explain or point at a field that is open. It does not operate Salesforce or export reports for you.

faq.question: Is it safe to show Lazur customer records?
faq.answer: Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Still, check your employer's rules on customer data before you show customer records.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with Jira on a Mac?
faq.answer: Lazur has no partnership with Atlassian, and it does not operate Jira for you. Atlassian says support has ended for the Jira Cloud Mac app, so Jira runs in a browser. Lazur can explain what is on screen in that browser window.

faq.question: Is Lazur available on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

costs.title: Hours lost to repeat conversations
costs.text: The same priority question returns in every sync and every Slack thread. Each round costs time that could go to shipping or to deals. Salesforce's State of Sales blog says reps spend 60% of their time on non-selling tasks. That figure covers reps, not product managers, so use it as context only.

costs.title: Trust, credit and exclusion
costs.text: Forrester's interviews surfaced friction, exclusion and credit-stealing between teams. Its blog also cites a significant lack of communication, teamwork and trust. Once sales thinks product ignores its deals, every later request becomes a fight. Product also loses the context it needs to say yes well.

costs.title: Burnout on both sides
costs.text: Gallup reports that 76% of employees experience burnout at least sometimes. It reports that 28% say they are burned out very often or always. The article is dated March 13, 2020, and gives no survey year or sample size. Its top correlates include unclear communication from managers and unreasonable time pressure.

costs.title: A leadership blind spot
costs.text: Forrester's 2024 Priorities Survey found 82% of C-level B2B leaders say product, sales and marketing are aligned. That is a view from the top, and it covers all three teams, not product and sales alone. Frontline people feel the gap every week. When leaders miss it, nobody budgets time to fix it.

costs.title: Collaboration drag on roadmaps
costs.text: HBR's June 2024 article, citing Gartner, says 78% of leaders report collaboration drag. It describes that drag as too many meetings, too much peer feedback and unclear decision-making authority. Each of those drains attention, and none of them appears on a roadmap.

causes.title: Nobody owns the call
causes.text: HBR's June 2024 article names unclear decision-making authority as a driver of stalled collaboration. When nobody can say no, every request becomes a debate. Sales asks in Slack, product answers on a call, and the decision lives in someone's memory. One named owner per priority is the first repair.

causes.title: Too many meetings and feedback loops
causes.text: The same HBR article describes too many meetings and too much peer feedback as drags on cross-functional work. A new meeting feels like progress. It often adds another place where decisions slip. A sharp meeting with a written outcome is easier to act on than a long, open-ended one.

causes.title: Outside pressure makes friction worse
causes.text: Forrester names technology advances, shifting buyer behavior and evolving business models as external pressures. It says they could worsen existing dysfunction. When buyers change faster than the roadmap, sales needs answers sooner than product can give them.

causes.title: Weak communication, teamwork and trust
causes.text: Forrester's blog cites a significant lack of communication, teamwork and trust, based on its interviews. That blog is about sales and marketing, not product. The same pattern can show up between product and sales. When trust is low, people protect their own goals and share less context.

causes.title: Work that defaults to coordination
causes.text: Pragmatic Institute's 2025 State of Product Management and Marketing Report says much of the time AI and automation saved is absorbed by coordination and alignment. Its page says work can default to coordination, opinion and acceleration without clarity. Clarity has to be built on purpose.

causes.title: Different scorecards
causes.text: Sales is often measured on bookings in a period. Product is often measured on what ships. When the scorecards differ, each team reads the same request differently. Ask what each team is measured on, and write that next to the priority list.

fixes.title: Name one owner for each priority
fixes.text: Put one name next to each priority in one shared place. Sales should know who to ask about scope and timing. If two people think they own a priority, nobody does. Review the owners at the weekly sync, and change them in writing.

fixes.title: Keep a decision log
fixes.text: Start one log in Notion or Google Sheets. Use columns for the request, the decision, the reason, the owner and the date. Add a row each time you say yes, no or later. The reason matters most, because it stops a request from coming back with no context.

fixes.title: Run one weekly sync with a fixed agenda
fixes.text: Keep the agenda the same every week. Cover blocked deals, new requests, log updates and what shipped. Decide each request in the room, or set a date for the decision. Read the decisions back out loud before the meeting ends.

fixes.title: Route requests through one channel
fixes.text: Pick one Slack channel for sales requests, and ask sales to post there. Requests in direct messages are hard for the next person to find. Pin a short rule to the top of the channel. The rule should say where requests go and where decisions live.

fixes.title: Close the loop with sales
fixes.text: Tell sales what shipped, what changed and why a request waited. Post the note in the channel where they asked. A short note is easier to act on than a long status update. It also gives sales something accurate to repeat to customers.

fixes.title: Say no in writing, with a reason
fixes.text: A no with a reason gives sales something to work with. Name the priority the request conflicts with, and give a date to revisit. For example: we are not taking this on this quarter because onboarding is the top priority, and we will look again on the date below.

fixes.title: Pick an alignment model on purpose
fixes.text: Forrester's blog lists four models: siloed, assimilated, subservient and proportionate. The blog is about sales and marketing, so treat it as a starting frame rather than a rule for product. Pick one model, write it down, and review it once a quarter.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Pick the top priorities
plan.text: Open the shared priority list and write one owner next to each item. If an item has no owner, mark it as open. Send the list to the sales lead with one question: what is blocking your top open deal?

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Create the decision log
plan.text: Make one Notion database or Google Sheet with the request, decision, reason, owner and date. Add last week's requests from Slack. In Google Sheets, use Data > Create a filter to sort by owner.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Route requests to one channel
plan.text: Pick one Slack channel for sales requests and post a short rule at the top. Requests go in the channel, and decisions go in the log. Hold ⌥⌘ over any long thread and ask Lazur what was decided.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Run the weekly sync
plan.text: Hold the sync with a fixed agenda: blocked deals, new requests, log updates and shipped work. Decide each request in the room, or set a date. Write the reason down before anyone leaves the call.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Close the loop with sales
plan.text: Post what shipped and what changed in the sales channel. Name each request you said no to, and the reason. Hold fn to dictate the note, then read it before you send it.
